## The Source Base, The Pool replaced by a methods and contamination statement (line 930)

Before:

````
### The Pool

**4 sweeps retrieved 35,837 records of which 30,647 were distinct.** The shared rejection store removed 1,829. The subject gate admitted 9,012 and refused 19,806. Deduplication by title and year removed a further 383, leaving 8,596 records across 15 clusters. The 7 October rebuild refused a further 157, leaving 8,439, and the 8 October second sampling pass refused 18 more, leaving 8,421, and the removal of 38 records that are notices or parts of works rather than works left **8,383 records, every one of which is cited**. A further 153 definitions are hand-written, being 77 primary documents and encyclopaedic anchors, 14 books whose identifiers were each resolved and read back against both the title and the author claimed for them, and 62 back-references to earlier articles in this series.

By source the admitted set is 7,804 from the Crossref registry, 906 from the NASA technical reports server and 302 through the Defense Technical Information Center's registry prefix. **1,190 of the 8,383 records the survey now holds, 14.2 percent, are report primaries.**

**The gate was rebuilt on 7 October 2026, after the counts first published with this article, and it refused 157 records that shared a word with this subject and nothing else.** 82 were about road vehicles, being driving simulators, automotive head-up displays, the steering and suspension of cars, the Calspan tyre research facility and the Calspan and Chrysler research safety vehicle, and 21 were clinical medicine, among them studies of neuromuscular disease, stroke rehabilitation and dyslexia. The remainder were 12 on other fields such as integrated circuit layout and the biomechanics of rising from a chair, 9 on computer hard disk drives, 9 on agriculture, water treatment, batteries and oceanography, 7 on coupled oscillators in physics and biology, 6 on railways, 6 on unrelated physics and remote sensing, 3 on epidemiology and 2 on speech processing. **The survey went from 8,596 records to 8,439.** The clusters most changed are the instrument, which lost 36 records and almost all of them driving simulators, the human being deceived, which lost 29, and the autonomy the X number was for, which lost 16. A reading of 300 records that neither screen had flagged found 5 off topic, which put the contamination near 1.7 percent before the rebuilt patterns were swept, and all 5 fall under patterns the rebuild then swept, so that sample drove its own sweep and could not measure what remained after it.

**A second seeded sample of 300 records that no earlier reading had seen, drawn on 8 October 2026, found 7 off topic**, being a servo for computer hard disk drives, an audiology test of speech recognition, the longitudinal control of a car, a biofouling study of underwater gliders, a head-up display for diving rebreathers, a pollution-control problem in economics and a peer review of a study of human walking. Sweeping those homonyms and their neighbours through the whole survey removed 11 more, 18 in all, of which 8 were about road vehicles, 2 about hard disk drives, 2 about underwater gliders, 2 were peer reviews of the walking study, and 1 each concerned audiology, rebreathers, pollution economics and the allocation of satellite communications bandwidth. **The survey went from 8,439 records to 8,421.** That sample measured 7 in 300, or 2.33 percent, in the 8,439 records it was drawn from. **It drove its own sweep, so it does not measure what remains in the 8,421**, and no figure for that remainder is claimed. **Later on 8 October 2026 a further 38 records were removed because they are not works**, being 30 correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, 3 decision letters, reviewer reports and author responses, and 5 figure and supplementary-material records, found by a rule that reads each title's opening words and each identifier's form, which took the survey from 8,421 records to 8,383.
````

After:

````
### What the Survey Admits

**The survey admits a record when its title matches this article's subject vocabulary.** Its 8,383 research records come from the Crossref registry, the NASA technical reports server and the Defense Technical Information Center, and every one of them is cited. A person has read the titles that the exclusion patterns flag and a random sample of the rest, and records read as off topic, and others of their kinds, are removed. **1,190 of the 8,383 records, 14.2 percent, are report primaries.** A further 153 definitions are hand-written, being 77 primary documents and encyclopaedic anchors, 14 books and 62 back-references to earlier articles in this series.

**Several of this subject's words also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word is excluded.** The excluded literatures are road vehicles and their drivers, among them driving simulators, automotive head-up displays, the steering and suspension of cars, the Calspan tyre research facility and the Calspan and Chrysler research safety vehicle, together with clinical medicine and rehabilitation, computer hard disk drives, coupled oscillators in physics and biology, railways, speech and audiology, underwater gliders, diving equipment, environmental economics, satellite communications, agriculture, water treatment, batteries, oceanography, integrated circuit layout and the biomechanics of rising from a chair. The general psychometric literature of measurement scales is outside the survey, while the literature on pilot rating scales themselves is inside it. Correction, erratum, retraction and withdrawal notices, decision letters, reviewer reports and author responses, and figure and supplementary-material records are excluded as well, because a survey counts research works and those are parts of works or editorial events rather than works.

**Three literatures that are contamination for other subjects are part of this one.** The human-factors literature of cockpit displays and symbology is on subject, because this subject is a pilot in a cockpit being deceived about which aeroplane is being flown, and the aircraft's own documented programme work is a programmable helmet-mounted display and a virtual head-up display. The curriculum literature of test pilot schools is on subject, because the aircraft is operated by a school and flown by its students. The physiology of pilot workload is on subject, because it is the discipline that measures a pilot, while clinical medicine is not.

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept.** Studies of human tracking under carbon monoxide, alcohol or flashblinding, and of tracking by primates, measure the human operator this subject models. Control design for plants other than aircraft, such as nuclear reactors, distillation columns, vehicle suspensions and rolling mills, uses the methods of model following and loop design, and the verification of autonomous ground vehicles sits beside the autonomy this aeroplane now hosts. Animal and insect flight is flight mechanics. Each is kept, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Not every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is an estimate from a sample.** The most recent measurement read 300 records drawn at random from those not previously read and found 7 off topic, or 2.33 percent, among them a servo for computer hard disk drives, an audiology test of speech recognition and the longitudinal control of a car. The records that sample exposed have been removed, together with others sharing their homonyms, so that figure overstates what remains by an unknown amount, and no later unread sample has been drawn.
````

## The Source Base, rejection-store subsections removed (Three Families, Omnibus Proceedings) (line 960)

Before:

````
### Three Families Were Opened and One of Them Was Split to Open It

The shared rejection store holds **141 curated patterns across 31 tagged families**. A tagged pattern is one whose subject is somebody else's subject, and an article whose subject it is may switch it off by name. **This article switched off 3**, and says so here because a filter switched off silently is indistinguishable from a filter that never existed.

**`cockpit-displays` was written by the X-50 article against the human-factors literature of rotorcraft displays**, as contamination of an article whose subject was unmanned. This article's subject is a pilot in a cockpit being deceived about which aeroplane is being flown, and the aircraft's own documented programme work is a programmable helmet-mounted display and a virtual head-up display. **The symbology and workload literature is the subject here and not the noise.** The X-59 article opened it for the same class of reason.

**`teaching` was deleting the curriculum this aeroplane exists to serve.** The family untagged removed `The USAF Test Pilot School flight control systems curriculum`, `Integrating UAS Flight Test Education Into the USAF Test Pilot School Curriculum` and `Simulator-Based Flight Test Engineering as a Capstone to the Dynamics and Control Curriculum`. **The aircraft is operated by a school and flown by its students**, so the pedagogical literature is on subject.

**`physiology` did not exist before this article and was created by splitting an entry rather than by widening a family.** The biomedical computational-fluid-dynamics entry earned by the X-51 article alternated ten terms, of which exactly one, the stem `physiolog`, names the discipline that measures a pilot. Untagged it removed `Physiological assessment of pilot workload in simulated and actual flight environments`, `Pilot Workload Analysis Based upon In-Flight Physiological Measurements`, `A Physiologically Based Model of Neuromuscular System Dynamics` and a study of simulator frame rate published in a physiology journal. **Opening the `medicine` family wholesale would have readmitted thirty-eight records on artificial intelligence in clinical trials**, so the alternative was separated into its own tagged entry on the X-55 article precedent. Two tests hold both halves, and the medical remainder that the split releases carries no aeronautical anchor and is refused by the gate downstream.

### An Omnibus Proceedings Volume Is a List of Subjects and Not a Subject

**The store reads a record's title and its container together, which is right, because a turbomachinery journal is real evidence that a paper is turbomachinery. It stops being right when the container is a numbered proceedings volume whose name concatenates its tracks.** One conference prints each year's proceedings as `Volume 2, Aircraft Engine, Marine, Microturbines and Small Turbomachinery, Oil and Gas Applications`, which names four unrelated fields, and that string alone removed `Integrated Flight and Propulsion Operating Modes for Advanced Fighter Engines` from an article about flight control.

**This is the X-57 article's multi-modal venue defect appearing in a different family**, and the repair has the same shape. The guard fires only when the container names a numbered volume alongside aeronautics, which is the signature of an omnibus proceedings and never of a turbomachinery journal. **A measurement of how often this class occurs found 137 records in this pool dropped by the container alone with a clean title**, most of them correctly, including a paper titled `Dogfight in the clouds` published in a volume on British archaeology in the Middle East. **The container filter earns its place and needs guarding, which are not in tension.**

````

After:

````
(removed)
````

## The Source Base, conclusions probe history and before and after table replaced (line 976)

Before:

````
### Do the Conclusions Have a Literature

**19 conclusions were probed twice, once in this article's own words and once in the field's.** The gap between the two counts is the measurement, because a thin count under an article's own phrasing is a fact about the phrasing and not about the claim.

**The probe was run after the first sweep, four conclusions came back under twenty records in the field's own vocabulary, and a second sweep was aimed at three of them.** The fourth is a claim about documents rather than about aeroplanes and no sweep will help it. The column headed `before` is the first sweep's count and the column headed `after` is the present one, so the effect of the later sweeps is data rather than assertion. **10 of the 19 conclusions gained more than half again as much coverage.**

**The equation-density review then added seven conclusions and a third sweep followed**, which is this corpus's oldest and most reliable rule. An equation pass promotes subjects, and the harvest that preceded the draft could not know which derivations would come to exist, so the subjects a later pass promotes are systematically under-represented in the pool it drew on. **Five measured under seventy records after the pass had placed equations in them**, being describing functions, pilot rating scales as a measurement instrument, direct lift control, high-lift device scheduling and the characterisation of a divergent mode.

**The rating-scale sweep was aimed at the aeronautical slice and not at measurement theory.** The general psychometric literature carries no aeronautical anchor and the gate refuses it, correctly. What this article needs is the literature on pilot rating scales themselves, which is aeronautical, which the gate admits, and which is the part that bears on the claim.

**A fourth sweep followed for a different reason and its records are in the `after` column too.** It was written to raise the report-primary share rather than to cover a conclusion, so it is not the cause of the movements above and it is not separable from them either. **The column is what the pool holds now**, and no attempt is made to apportion the growth between the sweeps that produced it.

| a direct lift control is what lets a simulator imitate a different wing | 40 | 8 | 139 |
| the determinant of the longitudinal control matrix is proportional to the separation of the two surfaces' centres of pressure | 0 | 16 | 120 |
| a rate limit divided by a deflection limit is a frequency | 0 | 303 | 645 |
````

## The Source Base, registry yield subsection removed (line 1042)

Before:

````
### How the Two Registries Answered, Measured Rather Than Assumed

**The reports server is query-limited and the defence registry is ceiling-limited, and the remedy differs.** The fourth sweep logged its per-question yield so that the claim could be checked rather than repeated.

| Registry | Questions | Cap | Saturated | Mean yield |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| NASA technical reports server | 148 | 10 records | 90, 60.8 percent | 7.29 |
| Defense Technical Information Center | 42 | 200 rows | 42, 100.0 percent | 200.0 |

**Every one of the 42 defence-registry questions returned exactly 200 rows.** Not most of them. All of them. **A registry that saturates on every question is telling you that the binding constraint is entirely the number of questions and not their quality**, and that a better-worded question would have returned the same two hundred rows of something else.

**The reports server saturated on 60.8 percent and averaged 7.29 records against a cap of 10.** That is a different shape. **Roughly two questions in five came back under the cap**, which means those questions had genuinely exhausted what the server holds on their subject, and it is the only evidence in this article that any part of the sweep reached the bottom of anything.

**Only the fourth sweep logged this and the earlier three did not.** They printed a running total where this one printed an increment, and reading the earlier logs the same way gave a mean of three hundred records per question against a cap of ten. **An impossible number is the clearest sign that a parser is reading the wrong column**, and the measurement is restricted to the sweep that recorded it rather than extended to the ones that did not.

````

After:

````
(removed)
````

## The Source Base, programme papers restated without the search story (line 1057)

Before:

````
### The Programme's Own Index, Recovered by Walking a Numbering

**A thematic sweep found four of the programme's own papers and the conference's own numbering found eight.** Asking about the aeroplane returns the papers whose titles name the aeroplane. **It does not return the ones whose titles name the systems**, being the simulation system's design, the autonomy interface's design, the ground and flight testing of the simulation system, and the flight testing of the autonomy.

**Resolving every identifier in two contiguous ranges recovered all eight**, in two blocks of four, which is two conference sessions. This is the X-59 article's lesson repeated. That article established that a programme's own published index recovers what a thematic sweep cannot, and found that its programme published none. **This one publishes a session, and a session has a numbering.**

**The same walk turned up a correction notice on one of the eight**, which is a fact about the record rather than about the aeroplane. The article cites it and does not know what was corrected.
````

After:

````
### The Programme's Own Papers Form Two Sessions

**The programme published eight papers at the 2023 SciTech forum of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, and their identifiers fall in two contiguous blocks of four**, 1744 to 1747 and 1925 to 1928, which is the shape of two conference sessions. They cover the aeroplane's capabilities and architecture, the model-following algorithm and its control allocation, the design of the simulation system and its ground and flight testing, the design of the system for autonomous control of the simulation, the flight testing of the simulation and the autonomy, and a vision for accelerating autonomy test and evaluation on the aeroplane.

**The registry also records a correction notice on one of the eight**, which is a fact about the record rather than about the aeroplane. The article cites it and does not know what was corrected.
````
